The field discriminant criterion of [Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, p.47](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=47) therefore says the reduction has no repeated roots exactly when p does not divide its discriminant. The bracketed Fact hypothesis supplies primality; p is not an arbitrary modulus. Discriminants commute with coefficient maps for monic polynomials, as expected from [Cohen §3.3.2](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-02945-9)’s determinant construction. In a nontrivial target ring, monicity preserves degree, so the same matrix determinant is mapped. If the target is the zero ring, degree may drop but the equality is automatic. Thus the theorem correctly includes that boundary case. The discriminant is a signed determinant with matrix size determined by degree, following [Cohen §3.3.2](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-02945-9). The explicit equality of natural degrees lets coefficient mapping use the same indices and sign, giving discr(map f)=map(discr f). Degree loss is not silently permitted; degree zero, including zero polynomials, is covered by the empty determinant convention. For a nonzero polynomial over a field, normalization by its nonzero leading coefficient reduces the criterion to [Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, p.47](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=47)’s simple-root test; scaling changes the discriminant by a nonzero factor. The nonzero hypothesis is essential here: Lean defines the zero polynomial’s discriminant as 1, although zero is not separable. Checks pass: [integer discriminant 4](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Discriminant.lean#L896), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Discriminant.lean#L737), [integer nonseparability](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Discriminant.lean#L901).

Here p is prime and does not divide the leading coefficient. Consequently reduction to 𝔽ₚ preserves degree and remains nonzero. Applying [Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, p.47](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=47)’s field criterion turns nonzero discriminant modulo p into p∤discr(f). The leading-coefficient condition is necessary for this degree-preserving specialization and is not replaced by monicity. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Discriminant.lean#L798).

Over a field, the monic discriminant vanishes exactly when two roots coincide, matching [Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, p.47](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=47). Monicity already excludes the zero polynomial; over this field the Bézout definition of separability is equivalent to having distinct roots. The same nonzero-discriminant assertion over ℤ would fail, as the native X²−1 counterexample records. Checks pass: [integer discriminant4](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Discriminant.lean#L896), [integer nonseparability](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Discriminant.lean#L901).
The integer polynomial X²−1 has nonzero discriminant 4.
That same polynomial has no Bézout identity with its derivative over ℤ.

This criterion tests separability after passage to a certified fraction field. Monicity preserves degree and the fraction-field map is injective, so nonvanishing of the discriminant is unchanged; [Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, p.47](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=47) then applies. It does not claim Bézout separability over the original ring, where a nonzero discriminant need not be a unit. The hypothesis says the leading coefficient survives the map into a field. It ensures both degree preservation and a nonzero mapped polynomial, so coefficient compatibility and [Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, p.47](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=47) give the equivalence. No injectivity of the coefficient map is needed; reduction modulo a prime is an intended example. Equal natural degrees let these indices be identified, after which mapping coefficients gives the same matrix because derivatives and the prescribed replacement row commute with the map. The statement works over semirings and asserts matrix equality, with no invertibility or division assumption. The sign exponent is the integer number of unordered pairs; for the constant monic polynomial 1, both sides are 1. A homeomorphism stores a bijection together with continuity of both its forward and inverse maps. These are precisely the standard mathematical requirements. The inverse identities come from the underlying bijection, so inverse continuity is explicitly included. Arbitrary topological spaces are allowed, including empty spaces when a bijection between them exists. [Semmes Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L44).

The inverse of a homeomorphism is again a homeomorphism. The construction reverses the stored bijection and swaps the two continuity proofs; its forward map is exactly the original inverse. Consequently no new choice of inverse is involved, and applying this operation twice recovers the original homeomorphism. [Semmes Def.2.8.2 and following paragraph](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L80).

Composition takes a homeomorphism from X to Y and one from Y to Z to the homeomorphism from X to Z. The first argument is applied first: h₁.trans h₂ means h₂ after h₁. The inverse applies their inverses in reverse order, and continuity in both directions follows by composition. [Semmes Prop.2.8.1; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L115).

The identity function on any topological space is a homeomorphism from that space to itself. The construction uses the identity bijection for both directions, so both inverse identities and continuity hold directly. The two occurrences of the space carry the same topology, including when the space is empty. [Semmes Def.2.8.2 and following paragraph](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L110).

Self-homeomorphisms form a group under composition, with identity map as the identity element and inverse homeomorphism as group inverse. Multiplication is ordered by function composition: (f*g)(x)=f(g(x)), so g acts first. This explains the reversed use of the trans constructor, which lists the first-applied homeomorphism first. [Semmes Def.2.8.2 and following paragraph](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L171).

This condition says that every member of a supplied family of bijections is continuous in both directions. The implicit EquivLike assumption already supplies forward maps, inverses and their two inverse identities. Thus the two additional continuity requirements express exactly a family of homeomorphisms; they do not assert that the family contains every homeomorphism. [Semmes Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L495).

For an already specified function, being a homeomorphism is expressed as continuity, bijectivity and openness. For a bijection, sending open sets to open sets is precisely continuity of the inverse, so this predicate matches the standard definition. Including openness prevents a continuous bijection alone from being mistaken for a homeomorphism. [Semmes Defs.2.8.2–3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L552).

A function known to be continuous, open and bijective is packaged as a homeomorphism with the same forward map. Bijectivity determines its inverse uniquely, and openness ensures that inverse is continuous. Although the construction selects inverse values, its result agrees with the mathematically determined inverse rather than introducing arbitrary additional data. [Semmes Defs.2.8.2–3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L564).

A supplied bijection that is continuous and open becomes a homeomorphism without changing either underlying function. Openness gives continuity of its inverse because inverse images under that inverse are images under the original bijection. This is the standard open-bijection criterion and does not require compactness or separation assumptions. [Semmes Defs.2.8.2–3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L461).

A continuous closed bijection is a homeomorphism: images of closed sets are the inverse images under its inverse, proving inverse continuity. The construction retains the supplied bijection and inverse. Its formal hypothesis is closedness; the docstring’s openness formulation is equivalent for bijections, since bijections preserve complements. [Semmes Prop.2.7.9; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L475).

If a space is discrete, every space homeomorphic to it is also discrete. Every target subset has an open inverse image in the discrete source, and the inverse homeomorphism makes that subset open. The conclusion concerns the topology already supplied on the target, rather than replacing it by a newly chosen topology. [Semmes §1.1.1; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L252).

A homeomorphism sends the interior of a set exactly to the interior of its image. Openness gives the forward inclusion, and applying the same argument to the inverse gives the reverse inclusion. Interiors are taken in the respective ambient spaces, and the subset need not itself be open or closed. [Semmes Def.1.4.9; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L310).

A homeomorphism carries the boundary of a subset exactly onto the boundary of its image. Here frontier means closure minus interior in the ambient space. Preservation of closure and interior, together with bijectivity preserving set differences, gives the equality. No closedness of the subset or separation condition on the spaces is assumed. [Semmes §1.4; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L316).

A homeomorphism sends the closure of any subset onto the closure of its image. Continuity gives one inclusion, and continuity of the inverse gives the other. The closures are taken in the original ambient spaces, so this applies equally to dense, closed, or empty subsets without additional separation assumptions. [Semmes Def.1.4.7; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L304).

Taking an inverse image under a homeomorphism commutes with taking interior. Continuity makes the inverse image of the target interior open, and openness of the homeomorphism gives the opposite inclusion. Both interiors use the given ambient topologies; the statement makes no assumption that the target subset is open. [Semmes Def.1.4.9; Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L307).

The inverse image of a subset’s boundary under a homeomorphism is the boundary of its inverse image. Frontier is closure minus interior, and inverse images preserve set differences while this map also preserves closure and interior. These are ambient boundaries in the two spaces, with no regularity assumption on the subset. [Semmes §1.4; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L313).

A homeomorphism takes every closed subset of its source to a closed subset of its target. The image is the inverse image under the continuous inverse map, so the usual closed-preimage criterion applies. This establishes an ambient closed-image property, with no compactness or Hausdorff assumptions needed. [Semmes Prop.2.7.9; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L293).

A homeomorphism sends open source sets to open target sets because their images are inverse images under its continuous inverse. The declaration therefore gives exactly the standard open-map property. It concerns openness in the whole target space, not merely relative openness in a smaller image; the homeomorphism is onto. [Semmes Defs.2.8.2–3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L280).

Every homeomorphism is an embedding: it is injective, and the topology on its domain is exactly the topology pulled back from its target. Continuity in both directions gives that equality of topologies. The statement forgets surjectivity while retaining the stronger embedding condition, rather than merely retaining continuity and injectivity. [Semmes §1.5; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L250).

A homeomorphism identifies its domain with an open subspace of the target. It is already an embedding, and its range is the entire target, which is open. Thus the stated open-embedding conclusion matches the standard inherited-topology meaning, without asserting that an arbitrary continuous injection has open image. [Semmes §1.5; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L295).

A homeomorphism is a closed embedding: it identifies the source with its range in the inherited topology, and that range is the whole target, hence closed. This uses the standard embedding and closed-range conditions. Neither compactness of the source nor a Hausdorff condition on the target is required. [Semmes §1.5.1; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L298).

A homeomorphism is a quotient map because it is onto and a target subset is open exactly when its inverse image is open. Continuity gives one direction of this criterion, and inverse continuity gives the other. Thus the target’s existing topology is exactly the quotient topology determined by the map. [Semmes §5.6.1; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L243).

A homeomorphism is an open quotient map: it is surjective, continuous, and sends open sets to open sets. These are precisely the three requirements stored in the formal property. The openness follows from continuity of the inverse, so the result preserves the distinction between ordinary quotient maps and open quotient maps. [Semmes Def.2.8.3; §5.6.1](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L282).

A function on Y is continuous exactly when its composite with a homeomorphism from X to Y is continuous. Composition proves one direction; composing back with the continuous inverse proves the other. The homeomorphism is applied first, and the equivalence tests continuity on the whole domain Y, not only on a subset. [Semmes Prop.2.8.1; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L324).

The image of a subset under a homeomorphism equals its inverse image under the inverse homeomorphism: a target point belongs exactly when its unique preimage lies in the subset. This is a set-theoretic consequence of bijectivity, valid for every subset, and explains how continuity of the inverse controls images. [Semmes Def.2.8.2; §2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L232).

A homeomorphism transports the neighborhood filter at x exactly to the neighborhood filter at its image. Continuity supplies convergence, while the continuous inverse supplies the reverse comparison. The transported filter consists of sets whose inverse images are source neighborhoods, matching the standard pushforward definition; it is not a pointwise image of individual points. [Semmes §§7.1.1,7.2.1](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L401).

A target subset is open exactly when its inverse image under a homeomorphism is open. Continuity of the forward map proves one direction; continuity of the inverse and surjectivity recover the subset in the other. This expresses equality of the transported topologies, for arbitrary subsets and arbitrary topological spaces. [Semmes Prop.2.7.9; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L273).

A homeomorphism pulls the target topology back to exactly the existing source topology. This follows from continuity in both directions: target open sets pull back to open source sets, and every open source set arises this way. The conclusion describes equality of topologies, rather than merely the inequality sufficient for continuity. [Semmes Prop.2.7.9; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Defs.lean#L238).

A dense inducing map has dense range and gives its domain exactly the topology pulled back from the target. These two stored conditions combine ordinary density with the inherited-topology requirement. Injectivity is not included, so different domain points may be identified if their neighborhoods cannot distinguish them; a dense subspace inclusion is the familiar example. [Semmes Def.1.3.1; §1.5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/DenseEmbedding.lean#L37).

This construction chooses a limit of f along preimages of neighborhoods of each target point, with an arbitrary fallback if no limit exists. It need not actually extend f without further hypotheses. The source’s Hausdorff uniqueness theorem confirms that, whenever a continuous extension exists, the construction equals that extension. [Semmes §§7.1.5,7.2.1](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/DenseEmbedding.lean#L139).

For a dense inducing map, the closure of the image of any neighborhood of a is a neighborhood of its image. Pullback topology provides a target open neighborhood whose preimage lies in the original set; density puts that target neighborhood inside the closure of its image. Taking closure is essential to this conclusion. [Semmes Def.1.3.1; §1.5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/DenseEmbedding.lean#L66).

Two continuous functions into a Hausdorff space that agree on a dense range agree everywhere. Their equality set is closed and contains the dense range, hence the whole domain. The map supplying that range needs neither continuity nor injectivity; its source is merely a set, with no topology assumed. [Semmes Def.1.3.1; §1.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/DenseEmbedding.lean#L380).

A property holding on a dense range holds at every point if its truth set is closed. The closed truth set contains the closure of that range, which is the whole space. This is a topological density argument, and it requires no topology or continuity for the map’s source. [Semmes Def.1.3.1; Prop.1.4.8](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/DenseEmbedding.lean#L358).

This finite set lists the positive divisors of a natural number. For a positive input it gives the usual divisor set, including one and the number itself. At zero it is deliberately empty, although every natural number divides zero; this is a finite-set convention. Compared with [Aspnes §§8.1,8.3](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Divisors.lean#L53).

Membership means that the candidate divides the given natural number and that this number is nonzero. Thus ordinary divisibility alone is insufficient at zero, where the chosen divisor set is empty. No separate positivity assumption on the candidate is needed: divisibility of a nonzero natural number supplies it. Compared with [Aspnes §8.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Divisors.lean#L110).

The divisor set of zero is empty by definition. This does not say that zero has no divisors: every natural number divides zero, so its unrestricted divisor collection would be infinite. The empty-set convention keeps the divisor operation finite and makes sums over this particular set equal zero. Compared with [Aspnes §§8.1,6.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Divisors.lean#L245).

The finite divisor set of one consists of one alone. In natural numbers, a product equals one only when both factors are one, so neither zero nor any larger natural number can occur. The declaration includes one itself, unlike the separate notion of proper divisors. Compared with [Aspnes §8.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Divisors.lean#L267).

Every member of a natural number’s finite divisor set is positive. For a nonzero dividend this follows because zero cannot divide it; for dividend zero there are no members, so the implication is vacuous. The statement concerns membership in the chosen finite set, not arbitrary divisibility of zero. Compared with [Aspnes §8.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Divisors.lean#L274).

A member of the finite divisor set divides the original natural number. This is the forward direction of the membership characterization, so it remains valid without an explicit nonzero hypothesis. The converse needs that hypothesis: every natural number divides zero, while the chosen divisor set of zero is empty. Compared with [Aspnes §8.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Divisors.lean#L116).

This finite set records ordered factor pairs of a natural number: both coordinates are positive and their product is the number. Swapping unequal factors gives a different pair. The set is empty at zero. Its use of natural division is guarded by an exact product check, so rounding introduces no extra pairs. Compared with [Aspnes §8.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Divisors.lean#L66).

An ordered pair belongs to the factor-pair set exactly when its product equals the given natural number and that number is nonzero. Positivity of both coordinates then follows automatically. At zero even pairs whose product is zero are excluded, matching the declared empty-set convention rather than unrestricted factorization. Compared with [Aspnes §8.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Divisors.lean#L126).

For a prime p, summing a function over the divisors of p^k equals summing its values at 1,p,…,p^k. The upper exponent k is included; when k is zero there is just the term at one. The values need only an associative, commutative addition with zero. Compared with [Aspnes §§8.3,6.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Divisors.lean#L520).

A sum over the divisors of a prime p has exactly two terms, the function values at p and at one. Primality ensures these divisors are distinct. The function is arbitrary, and its values need only an associative, commutative addition with zero; no multiplicativity or division operation is assumed. Compared with [Aspnes §§8.3,6.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Divisors.lean#L475).

Converting a finite sum of natural numbers into an additive structure gives the sum of their converted values. The conversion sends n to n copies of one. An empty sum stays zero, and distinct indices with equal values still contribute separately. Injectivity of the conversion is not required. Compared with [Judson §§16.2–16.3](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/BigOperators/Ring/Finset.lean#L341).

Converting a finite sum of integers into an additive group gives the sum of their converted values. Negative integers are interpreted using additive inverses, and the empty sum stays zero. This identity also holds in positive characteristic, where different integers may have the same value after conversion. Compared with [Judson §§16.2–16.3](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/BigOperators/Ring/Finset.lean#L381).

Converting a finite product of natural numbers into a commutative semiring gives the product of the converted factors. The empty product is one on both sides, and zero factors remain zero. Neither subtraction nor characteristic zero is needed; the identity still holds when the conversion identifies different natural numbers. Compared with [Judson §16.3](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/BigOperators/Ring/Finset.lean#L346).

Converting a finite product of integers into a commutative ring gives the product of the converted factors. Negative factors retain their usual sign behavior, and an empty product becomes one. The formula requires commutative multiplication for the unordered product, but it does not require an injective conversion or characteristic zero. Compared with [Judson §16.3](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/BigOperators/Ring/Finset.lean#L386).

This is the canonical map from natural numbers into a semiring, sending n to n copies of one and preserving zero, one, addition and multiplication. Multiplication in the target need not be associative. The map need not be injective: in positive characteristic distinct natural numbers can have the same image. Compared with [Judson §§16.2–16.3](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Cast/Basic.lean#L61).

This is the canonical map from integers into a ring, using repeated addition of one for positive integers and additive inverses for negative integers. It preserves zero, one, addition and multiplication, even without associative multiplication. It need not be injective; positive characteristic can identify different integers. Compared with [Judson §§16.2–16.3](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/Cast/Lemmas.lean#L84).

The canonical natural-number map is injective under the explicit characteristic-zero assumption. Here that assumption means precisely that distinct natural numbers give distinct repeated sums of one. The target is allowed to be an additive monoid with one; in this generality that condition is stronger than just excluding positive sums equal to zero. Compared with [Judson §16.2](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/CharZero/Defs.lean#L65).

In an additive group with one and characteristic zero, converting integers is injective: equal converted values imply equal integers. Additive inverses handle negative inputs, so this extends the natural-number injectivity assumption to all integers. No multiplication or order on the target is required; positive characteristic is explicitly excluded. Compared with [Judson §16.2](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/Cast/Lemmas.lean#L68).

Natural-number conversion preserves multiplication: converting m*n gives the product of the converted m and n. This follows from distributing multiplication over repeated addition of one. The target may be a semiring without associative multiplication, and characteristic zero is unnecessary. Zero factors and conversions into the trivial semiring are included. Compared with [Judson §§16.1,16.3](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Cast/Basic.lean#L55).

Integer conversion preserves multiplication, including products involving negative integers. Repeated addition proves the natural cases, and additive inverses supply the sign rules. The target need only satisfy the ring laws with possibly nonassociative multiplication. No injectivity or order hypothesis is needed, so the statement also applies in positive characteristic. Compared with [Judson §§16.1,16.3](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Ring/Int/Defs.lean#L58).

Converting a natural-number power into a semiring gives the same result as first converting the base and then taking that power. The exponent is a natural number. Exponent zero gives one, including 0^0, and no injectivity or characteristic-zero assumption is needed; multiplication may be noncommutative. Compared with [Judson §16.3](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Cast/Basic.lean#L80).

Converting an integer power into a ring gives the power of the converted integer. Negative bases are allowed, but the exponent is a natural number, so no inverse operation is involved. The zero exponent gives one, including 0^0. Characteristic zero and commutative multiplication are not required. Compared with [Judson §16.3](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Ring/Int/Defs.lean#L73).

If one natural number divides another, their images in any semiring retain that divisibility: the converted natural-number witness still supplies the factor. Only the forward implication is asserted. The converse can fail, for example in the rationals, where two divides one. Zero divisors and positive characteristic are allowed. Compared with [Judson §§16.1,16.3](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Cast/Basic.lean#L85).

Every natural-number coefficient commutes with every element of the target semiring: n*x=x*n after converting n to repeated addition of one. This does not require the whole multiplication to be commutative, or even associative. Distributivity and the two identity laws suffice, including at n=0. Compared with [Judson §16.1](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Cast/Commute.lean#L44).

Every integer coefficient commutes with every element of a ring, even if multiplication is noncommutative or nonassociative. Positive coefficients are repeated sums of one; negative coefficients use additive inverses, which preserve the same commutation identity. The statement includes zero and imposes no characteristic-zero requirement on the ring. Compared with [Judson §16.1](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/Cast/Lemmas.lean#L93).

This natural-valued cardinality counts elements of a finite type and returns zero for every infinite type. Thus zero can mean either empty or infinite; it is not an infinite cardinal. The definition needs no chosen finite enumeration, and equivalent types receive the same value regardless of how their elements are represented. Compared with [Aspnes §§3.5.5.4,11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L39).

This counts all elements of a type equipped with a finite enumeration. The enumeration is a finite set, so each distinct element contributes once. Different enumerations give the same cardinality, and the empty type has cardinality zero. Infinite types are excluded by the required finite-enumeration structure, rather than assigned a default count. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Fintype/Card.lean#L40).

This is the number of distinct elements in a finite set. Its underlying list-like representation has no repetitions, so taking its length counts each element once and does not depend on order. The empty set has size zero and a singleton has size one, with no finiteness requirement on the surrounding type. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Finset/Card.lean#L47).

This is the cardinality of a finite multiset, counting repeated elements with their multiplicities. It is the length of any representing list; permuting that list preserves the result. Thus a multiset containing two copies of the same element has size two, unlike a finite set containing that element. Compared with [Aspnes §9.4.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Multiset/Defs.lean#L221).

The natural-valued cardinality is zero exactly when the type is empty or infinite. The second alternative is essential because this operation deliberately assigns zero to infinite types. For finite types alone, the statement reduces to the familiar fact that a set has zero elements precisely when it is empty. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L75).

The natural-valued cardinality is positive exactly when the type is both nonempty and finite. Nonemptiness alone is insufficient, since infinite types are assigned zero by this particular operation. This correctly recovers ordinary positive finite counting while making the default value outside the finite case explicit in both directions. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L80).

The natural-valued cardinality of integers modulo n is n. For positive n this is the usual count of residue classes. At n=0, the type is the integers themselves, which are infinite; its natural-valued cardinality is therefore zero by convention. The zero case does not claim a finite quotient. Compared with [Aspnes §§8.4,11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L247).

The natural-valued cardinality of a Cartesian product is the product of the two counts. This needs no finiteness assumptions: finite factors obey the usual counting rule, while an infinite factor makes the product either empty or infinite. In either case the convention assigning zero to infinite types keeps the formula valid. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.5](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L223).

For two finite types, the cardinality of their disjoint union is the sum of their cardinalities. Elements carry a left or right tag, so equal-looking values from the two sides remain distinct. Both finiteness assumptions matter: assigning zero to an infinite type would otherwise break the addition formula. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.3](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L217).

For finitely many indexed types, the count of choices of one element from each type is the product of their natural-valued counts. The indexed types themselves may be infinite, with zero used for infinite counts. An empty index set gives one choice and an empty product; an empty factor gives no choices. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.5](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L239).

For a finite domain, the number of functions into a finite codomain is the codomain’s size raised to the domain’s size. This formula also allows infinite codomains using the zero-count convention. An empty domain has exactly one function, so the zero-exponent convention, including 0^0=1, is essential. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L242).
